Financial planning · Deposit access and earlier bills · Visual planning guide

A higher deposit rate can meet an earlier bill only through a separate funding plan

Compare hypothetical cashable and locked deposits at the same end date, fund the same earlier bill and reconcile the interest cost of a separately assumed bridge loan.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare two hypothetical deposit contracts at the same end date

Interactive planning lab

Cashable route · cash at day 365 after the common bill$15,486.99
Locked deposit plus bridge · cash or shortfall at day 365$15,598.63
Locked-plus-bridge ending cash minus cashable ending cash$111.64

Original equal-end-date comparison, with the same initial deposit and same earlier bill. Hypothetical cashable terms permit principal-only partial withdrawal after thirty completed days; the remaining principal and accrued interest stay until day 365, when all interest is paid. Simple daily interest uses a 365-day year: full principal for the selected completed days, then remaining principal for 365 minus those days. The locked deposit releases nothing before day 365 and earns simple annual interest for the full year. Its bill is funded only by an independently assumed available bridge advance equal to that bill; simple bridge interest and principal are paid together at day 365. Credit availability is a prerequisite, not an automatic response to a cash gap. No fees, minimum remaining-balance rule, taxes, compounding, rollover, changing rates or additional borrowing is modeled. A negative settlement endpoint requires outside cash. No actual issuer’s withdrawal terms, credit approval or product offer is established.

On this page

  1. Confirm access before comparing a quoted rate
  2. Apply the cashable rate to the principal that remains
  3. Treat the bridge as a separate prerequisite and liability

The central idea

A maturity amount cannot fund an earlier bill by itself. Compare the cash available after the bill and all loan settlement, using the actual withdrawal and credit terms.

01

Confirm access before comparing a quoted rate

The FCAC’s GIC and term-deposit disclosure guide identifies principal and interest payment terms, charges, and whether early cashing is possible. It also describes disclosure of net proceeds and charges before an allowed early redemption.

That information requirement does not establish that a locked product can be broken. The two contracts in this model are independently authored assumptions. No bank’s withdrawal permission, minimum balance, interest treatment or product rate is imported.

Both routes begin with CAD 20,000 and must fund the same CAD 5,000 bill after ninety completed days. They finish at day 365. The comparison includes only these defined cash flows. It cannot replace checking the actual contract or deciding how much accessible cash the household needs for other purposes.

02

Apply the cashable rate to the principal that remains

The hypothetical cashable contract pays 3% simple annual interest on daily principal. It permits a principal-only partial withdrawal after thirty completed days. The model assumes all accrued interest is paid at day 365, with no withdrawal fee or change in the selected rate.

The first ninety days earn interest on CAD 20,000. The CAD 5,000 withdrawal then pays the bill, leaving CAD 15,000 to earn interest for the remaining 275 days. Interest across those two intervals totals approximately CAD 486.99.

Ending cash is therefore approximately CAD 15,486.99: remaining principal plus the modeled interest. The interest had not been received when the earlier bill was due, so it is not counted as part of that bill’s funding. Actual cashable products can have different withdrawal and interest rules; these particular assumptions need independent confirmation before use.

03

Treat the bridge as a separate prerequisite and liability

The locked contract pays 4.5% simple interest for the full year and releases nothing earlier. It returns CAD 20,900 at day 365. That larger maturity amount alone cannot pay the day-ninety bill.

The second route assumes a separately available CAD 5,000 bridge advance funds that bill. At an assumed 8% simple annual rate over 275 days, bridge interest is approximately CAD 301.37. Both loan principal and interest become payable at day 365.

After repaying CAD 5,301.37 from maturity proceeds, approximately CAD 15,598.63 remains. The waterfall deducts the loan settlement once. It does not deduct the earlier bill again because the bridge advance already funded it. If the assumed credit is unavailable, this locked-deposit route cannot fund the earlier bill as modeled.

04

Compare the actual interest paths, not two untouched deposits

The locked-plus-bridge route finishes approximately CAD 111.64 ahead in the default, before fees and taxes. The shared initial principal and shared bill cancel when the two ending balances are compared.

The interest bridge explains the remainder: CAD 900 of locked interest less approximately CAD 486.99 of cashable interest gives about CAD 413.01. Subtract approximately CAD 301.37 of bridge interest, leaving the CAD 111.64 difference.

Using CAD 600 as cashable interest would be inconsistent with this scenario. That would assume the entire CAD 20,000 stayed invested for the full year, even though CAD 5,000 funded the earlier bill. Likewise, comparing only the two deposit rates would omit the separate borrowing cost. Keep the amount invested, withdrawal date and funding route consistent throughout the comparison.

05

Test timing and borrowing cost while holding the bill constant

The matrix varies the completed days before the bill and the simple bridge rate. Initial principal, the bill percentage and both deposit rates stay selected. Each signed cell is locked-plus-bridge ending cash minus cashable ending cash at the common day-365 endpoint.

A later bill shortens the borrowing interval but also leaves more principal earning the cashable rate before withdrawal. The calculation includes both effects. Changing the bill’s percentage changes how much principal leaves the cashable deposit and how much the bridge must advance.

A positive cell is an arithmetic advantage under the chosen assumptions, not proof of an available or suitable strategy. Fees, taxes, changing rates or repayment conditions can change the result. A negative locked-route endpoint means additional outside cash is required at settlement; the model does not create further borrowing to fill it.

06

Build the payment plan from confirmed net amounts and dates

For an actual decision, confirm whether partial withdrawal is permitted, how it changes interest, when interest is paid, and what charges or minimum balances apply. Obtain the expected net amount rather than assuming the headline deposit rate determines the withdrawal proceeds.

Confirm any separate funding source before relying on it. Its amount, fees, interest convention, payment dates and maturity need to match the bill and deposit dates. Paying interest regularly or repaying principal earlier would require different cash flows from the single settlement modeled here.

The example uses a fixed 365-day year, simple interest, no fees and no tax. It does not model rollovers, emergency access rights or lending approval. Its purpose is to compare equal starting resources, the same expense and a common finish date while making the cost and availability of the earlier funding explicit.
